claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has an inherent, naturally formed oxide layer.
Air annealing at 700–900 °C for 10–100 hours can modify the thickness of the oxide scale on Q235 steel.
Air annealing at 700–900 °C for 10–100 hours can modify the phase composition of the oxide scale on Q235 steel.
Air annealing at 700–900 °C for 10–100 hours can modify the adhesion of the oxide scale on Q235 steel.
The annealing-formed oxide scale is expected to be predominantly iron-rich, with possible incorporation of minor elements.
A uniform and well-adherent pre-formed oxide scale acts as a barrier to corrosive species during high-temperature molten-salt exposure.
Excessive oxide-scale thickness can promote internal stress and spallation.
Oxide-scale spallation exposes the Q235 substrate and accelerates corrosion.
Oxide-scale uniformity and integrity mediate the temperature dependence of Q235 corrosion behavior.
Q235 samples having an optimized, uniform, and adherent annealing-formed scale will exhibit lower mass change during high-temperature molten-salt exposure than as-received Q235.
Q235 samples having an optimized, uniform, and adherent annealing-formed scale will exhibit less surface degradation and spallation during high-temperature molten-salt exposure than as-received Q235.
Annealing will produce only minimal differences in Q235 corrosion behavior during room-temperature salt exposure.
The as-received Q235 oxide may be less controlled in thickness, uniformity, and adhesion than an oxide produced by controlled annealing.
The proposed mechanism applies to controlled annealing and subsequent exposure to aggressive molten salts at 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when substantially different exposure conditions, doping, or mechanical pretreatments dominate oxidation kinetics.
